findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State explicitly in the plan which ports are 'default' for the normalisation (80 for http, 443 for https; all other port numbers are retained verbatim) so the helper's behaviour is unambiguous for on-premises DC URLs on non-standard ports.
evidence: 'default port dropped' — no definition of which port numbers qualify as default.
DC is 'commonly served at /jira' but could equally be served on port 8080 in many on-premises deployments.
findings.finding: The normalisation spec states 'default port dropped' but does not define which ports are considered 'default'. The HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) defaults are conventional but unstated; a non-standard port such as 8080 on an on-premises DC deployment is ambiguous — an executor could either keep or drop it. This is a minor defaultable gap under E2 signal 2.
findings.location: Context / Problem section: 'instance is derived from the CONFIGURED base URL — normalised (scheme dropped, host lowercased, default port dropped, trailing slash dropped, context path retained)'
scenarios: Two spellings of the same DC deployment — `http://jira.corp.com:80/jira` and `http://jira.corp.com/jira` — are expected to normalise to the same instance; the plan's own equivalence test requires this, but the rule is not stated for every scheme.

An executor drops port 8443 (HTTPS non-standard) thinking it is 'default for HTTPS on internal proxies', yielding an instance string that differs from `https://jira.corp.com:8443/jira` vs `https://jira.corp.com/jira`.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence: 'Default port means 80 for http:// and 443 for https://; any other port number is retained in the normalised instance string.'

findings.finding: The plan declares `remote_ref(self, remote_id: str) -> RemoteRef` on the `Backend` Protocol and implements it on both concrete backends, but the plan simultaneously and explicitly prohibits adding any production consumer ('NO INVENTED CONSUMER', 'no `remote_ref()` call is added to any pass'). A Protocol method with zero current production callers satisfies no current done-definition and is a YAGNI/premature-abstraction by the rubric's Rule-of-Three standard. The fake already implements it, but that asymmetry only matters if the Protocol is actually checked at runtime via `isinstance` — which requires a caller that never exists in this story.
findings.location: Approach section — 'NO INVENTED CONSUMER' and 'THE RECEIVER IS A `remote_ref()` MEMBER ON THE `Backend` PORT'; AC line 'no `remote_ref()` call is added to any pass'
scenarios: An implementer adds `remote_ref()` to the Protocol and both backends; the method is never called in any production pass. A later reviewer sees a declared Protocol member with no call-sites and correctly questions whether it should be removed, creating churn.

If the Protocol is `@runtime_checkable` and `remote_ref` is declared on it, any `isinstance(backend, Backend)` check now requires the method to be present — adding a conformance burden on every future backend implementation for a feature no current pass uses.

findings.finding: The plan's AC2 states 'both concrete backends IMPLEMENT `remote_ref()` and each returns a `RemoteRef` with a populated, non-empty `instance`' and also states 'the contract test constructs both real backends with NO ambient config.' These two constraints are mutually incompatible unless the contract test fixture explicitly passes an `instance` string to the backend constructors — but the plan does not specify this constructor-call change in `test_backend_contract.py`. The current fixture (`params=['fake', 'jira', 'jira-datacenter']`) constructs `JiraBackend(transport=FakeTransport())` and `JiraDataCenterBackend(transport=FakeTransport())` with no `instance`. If `instance` defaults to empty, the contract test backend's `remote_ref()` returns `instance=""`, failing AC2's non-empty assertion.
findings.location: AC2 / Testing section — 'BOTH REAL BACKENDS return a RemoteRef with a non-empty instance from remote_ref(), asserted against a real backend object' AND 'the contract test constructs those backends with NO ambient config'

findings.finding: The plan simultaneously asserts (a) the `instance` constructor parameter defaults to empty string, (b) the contract test constructs real backends with no config context and 'still passes', and (c) AC2 requires both real backends return a `RemoteRef` with a 'non-empty `instance`'. These three constraints cannot hold together: if the parameter defaults to `""`, the contract test fixture — which calls `JiraBackend(transport=FakeTransport())` and `JiraDataCenterBackend(transport=FakeTransport())` with no `instance` argument — will produce a `RemoteRef(instance="")`, which fails the non-empty assertion. The plan does not specify whether the fixture is updated to pass an explicit instance value (which would make the 'no config context' proof vacuous) or whether a different mechanism supplies a non-empty default.
findings.location: Approach section ('backends take the value as a constructor parameter (defaulting to empty)') + AC2 ('non-empty instance — asserted against the REAL backends') + Testing section ('contract test constructs those backends with NO ambient config and still passes')

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit statement (in Scope or Approach) that the `build_backend` factories call the normalisation helper on `settings.url` and pass the RESULT (the normalised instance string) to the backend constructor — not the raw URL.
evidence: Scope: 'both `build_backend` factories — pass `settings.url` in (they already resolve settings)'
AC1: 'a pure helper derives `instance` from a base URL; different deployments differ, and equivalent spellings of one deployment (trailing slash / case / default port) agree'
AC2: 'whose `instance` is EXACTLY THE VALUE THE CONSTRUCTOR WAS GIVEN'

If the factory passes the raw URL and the constructor stores it verbatim, AC1's equivalence guarantee is violated. If the constructor normalizes, AC2's 'exactly as given' language is violated. The call site of the helper is never named.
findings.finding: The Scope section says the `build_backend` factories 'pass `settings.url` in', implying the raw URL is passed to the constructor. But AC2 states the backend's `instance` is 'EXACTLY THE VALUE THE CONSTRUCTOR WAS GIVEN', and AC1 establishes that a normalisation helper transforms URLs (different spellings of the same deployment must agree). These two cannot both be true unless the factory calls the helper before passing — but the plan never says so. An implementer reading Scope literally passes the raw URL; one reading AC1+AC2 together must normalize in the factory. This is a cross-section contradiction between Scope and the AC pair.
findings.location: Scope section ('both `build_backend` factories — pass `settings.url` in') vs AC1 ('a pure helper derives `instance` from a base URL') vs AC2 ('EXACTLY THE VALUE THE CONSTRUCTOR WAS GIVEN')
scenarios: Implementer A reads Scope, passes raw URL to constructor, stores it verbatim — AC1 equivalence tests fail because 'http://JIRA.EXAMPLE.COM/' != 'jira.example.com/jira'.

Implementer B reads AC1+AC2, normalizes in the constructor before storing — AC2's 'exactly the value given' assertion passes trivially but the test no longer distinguishes constructor-storage from call-time resolution.
Implementer C normalizes in the factory — correct, but this is inferable only by triangulating three sections, never stated.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Scope bullet for `build_backend` factories, replace 'pass `settings.url` in' with 'call the normalisation helper on `settings.url` and pass the result as the `instance` constructor argument'.
